title: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp
source: Mauritshuis, The Hague, inv. 146 (public domain). Wikimedia Commons file: Rembrandt van Rijn - The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp - 146 - Mauritshuis.jpg (6000 x 4520 px; Mauritshuis inv. 146)
caption: Amsterdam, 1632: a famous doctor, a hanged thief, and an anatomy lesson that broke the rules. Can you spot how? #anatomy #medicalhistory #rembrandt #oilpainting #didyouknow
_verify: VERIFIED 2026-10-28, Mauritshuis (mauritshuis.nl/en/our-collection/artworks/146-the-anatomy-lesson-of-dr-nicolaes-tulp): inv. 146, oil on canvas, 169.5 x 216.5 cm, signed 'Rembrant. fv: 1632'; anatomy lesson of January 1632 for the Amsterdam surgeons' guild; 'Rembrandt was only twenty-five' when asked; the corpse is Adriaen Adriaensz, alias Aris Kindt, 'arrested for stealing a winter coat and sentenced to death', hanged 31 January 1632; Tulp starts with the arm and hand, 'departing from customary practice': normally 'the abdominal cavity and the perishable bowels would be dissected first, followed by the head and limbs'; painted 'together with a few guild members who contributed towards the fee'; numbers and names on the sheet held by Hartman Hartmansz were added at the beginning of the 18th century, partly reversed in a recent restoration that revealed Rembrandt's original drawing of an arm; Vesalius's frontispiece shows the author holding a dissected arm, Tulp may have wanted to emulate him; the work 'firmly established Rembrandt's name as a portraitist'.

VERIFIED, Wikipedia EN (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Anatomy_Lesson_of_Dr._Nicolaes_Tulp): Aris Kindt convicted of armed robbery, 'executed earlier on the same day'; lesson dated 31 January 1632; each sitter 'would have paid a certain amount of money to be included'; book in the lower right 'possibly' Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica (1543); 2006 Dutch recreation found 'several discrepancies' in the exposed forearm, a 2007 study read the white cord as the tendon of a variant forearm muscle; 1828 sale blocked by King William I, Dutch state bought it for 32,000 guilders for the Mauritshuis.
CONFLICTING, age: brief said 26; Mauritshuis says 25 (born July 1606, lesson January 1632). Slide 2 says 25. Wikipedia EN says 26.

CONFLICTING, crime: Mauritshuis says theft of a winter coat (elsewhere 'robbery'), Wikipedia 'armed robbery'. Slide 3 says 'a thief arrested for stealing a winter coat' (Mauritshuis wording). executedtoday.com notes a minority date of 16 January; Mauritshuis and Wikipedia give 31 January (not on the slide).
CAUTIOUS, 'hanged that morning': sources say only 'earlier on the same day'. Slide 3 says 'earlier that same day'.
CAUTIOUS, book = Vesalius: only 'possibly' (Wikipedia). Slide 5 says 'may be' and asks 'Was Tulp copying him?' (Mauritshuis: he 'may have wanted to emulate' Vesalius).
CAUTIOUS, who paid: Mauritshuis 'a few guild members who contributed towards the fee', Wikipedia says each sitter paid. Slide 6 says 'they chipped in'.
Slide 8 compresses the medical debate (2006 discrepancies vs 2007 variant muscle) into one line. No graphic description of the dissection anywhere.

slides.headline: This anatomy lesson broke the rules. Why?
slides.sub: Rembrandt, The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp, 1632

slides.headline: Amsterdam, 1632
slides.text: Amsterdam, 1632. The surgeons' guild asks Rembrandt, just 25, to paint its yearly public dissection. But look closely: this lesson breaks the rules.

slides.headline: The man on the table
slides.text: First, the man on the table: Aris Kindt, a thief arrested for stealing a winter coat. He was hanged earlier that same day.

slides.headline: Why the arm?
slides.text: Now Dr Tulp, forceps in hand, points to the forearm. That's the odd part: by custom, the abdomen came first, then head and limbs.

slides.headline: The book at his feet
slides.text: Why break the rules? The giant book at the feet may be Vesalius's anatomy, whose author posed holding a dissected arm. Was Tulp copying him?

slides.headline: Paying for a front seat
slides.text: Meanwhile, look at the faces crowding in. These surgeons weren't random onlookers: they chipped in to be painted here, beside the star doctor.

slides.headline: The name list
slides.text: But one surgeon holds a sheet that once listed their names. Rembrandt didn't write them: they were added around 1700, over his drawing of an arm, now visible again.

slides.headline: Is the arm right?
slides.text: And doctors still argue. A 2006 recreation found mismatches with a real arm; a 2007 study blamed a rare muscle variant, not Rembrandt.

slides.headline: The painting that made him
slides.text: It made Rembrandt's name. In 1828 the king stopped its sale; the state bought it. Would you have paid to stand there?
